units.t: Deciding Well Under Pressure.
Part one. One-way and two-way doors.
Every day you make hundreds of decisions.
Most are tiny, like which lane to take or what to have for lunch.
A few are big, like a job offer, a move interstate, or a car you'll be paying off for five years.
This lesson gives you a small toolkit for both, especially when you're under pressure.
The first tool is a single question.
Can I undo this?
Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon, put it memorably in his 2015 letter to shareholders.

He wrote that some decisions are consequential and irreversible or nearly irreversible, one-way doors, and these decisions must be made methodically, carefully, slowly, with great deliberation and consultation.
But most decisions aren't like that, he went on.
They are changeable, reversible.
They're two-way doors.
Here's the part people often miss.
Bezos wasn't mainly warning about rushing the big decisions.
He was warning about the opposite.
Many people, and many organisations, treat every two-way door as if it were a one-way door.
They agonise over small, fixable choices, and the result is slowness and missed chances.
So try sorting your decisions this way.
Trying a new gym, switching phone plans, testing a different route to work, rearranging the lounge room.
These are two-way doors.
If it doesn't work, you walk back through.
For these, decide quickly, learn from what happens, and adjust.
Selling a house, signing a long contract, saying something that can't be unsaid.
These are one-way doors.
For these, slow down on purpose.
The second tool comes from the economist and psychologist Herbert Simon, who later won a Nobel Prize.
In 1956 he coined a word that's worth knowing.
Satisficing.
It's a blend of satisfy and suffice.
A satisficer sets a standard of good enough, and picks the first option that meets it.
A maximiser keeps searching for the very best.
The psychologist Barry Schwartz and his colleagues have studied how these two styles play out.
In one study of university students looking for their first jobs, the maximisers ended up with starting salaries about twenty per cent higher.
But they felt worse about their jobs.
They were more stressed, more anxious and less satisfied with the outcome.
Searching for the best can win you a bit more, and still leave you feeling you've missed out.
So for everyday two-way doors, decide what good enough looks like before you start looking.
Then stop when you find it.
Part two. When the pressure's on.
Now for the hard part.
What happens to your thinking when the clock is ticking, or your heart is pounding?
In 1987, the Israeli psychologist Giora Keinan ran a study in which some people believed they might receive mild electric shocks while solving decision problems.
Under that stress, people were more likely to settle on an answer before they'd looked at all the options.
They also scanned the options less systematically, jumping around rather than working through them.
Stress doesn't just make us feel rattled.
It narrows what we look at.
That narrowing shows up in a quieter way too.
We often frame choices as yes or no.
Should I take this job or not?
Should we buy this house or not?
The management researcher Paul Nutt studied well over a hundred real decisions made in organisations.
When leaders only weighed a single option, whether or not, about half of those decisions were later judged failures.
When they compared two or more genuine alternatives, the failure rate dropped to about a third.
So one easy habit under pressure is to ask, what else could I do here?
Even one extra option widens the view.
And yet some people make excellent decisions under enormous pressure.
In the 1980s, the American psychologist Gary Klein studied fireground commanders, the officers who make life and death calls at burning buildings.
He expected them to be comparing options quickly.
Instead, most of the time they weren't comparing options at all.
They recognised the situation from experience, pictured the first sensible course of action playing out in their heads, and went with it unless they spotted a problem.
Klein called this recognition-primed decision making.
The lesson from Klein is that fast, confident decisions work well when you have real experience in that kind of situation.
An experienced nurse, mechanic or parent often knows what to do before they can explain why.
Your gut is trustworthy in areas where you've had lots of practice and quick feedback.
It's much less trustworthy in unfamiliar territory, like a first investment or a big career change.
So when you feel pressure on an unfamiliar decision, the first move is simple.
Check whether the deadline is real.
A salesperson saying the deal ends today is often creating pressure, not reporting it.
If the time pressure is genuine, take one slow breath out before you choose.
If it isn't, give yourself time.
Sleeping on a big decision is not weakness.
It's good practice.
The next tool is surprisingly powerful.
Ask yourself, what would I tell a friend to do?
In 2014, the psychologists Igor Grossmann and Ethan Kross studied what they called Solomon's paradox, named after the wise King Solomon, who was famously poor at running his own life.
People reasoned more wisely about a friend's relationship problem than about their own.
They were more open to other viewpoints and more aware of what they didn't know.
But when people imagined their own problem from a distance, as if it were happening to someone else, the gap disappeared.
Stepping outside yourself, even in your imagination, makes you wiser.
Part three. Testing a big decision.
For one-way doors, here are two final tests you can run in your head, right now, on the way to work.
The first is the ten-ten-ten test, popularised by the business writer Suzy Welch, who wrote a whole book about it in 2009.
Ask yourself three questions.
How will I feel about this decision in ten minutes?
In ten months?
And in ten years?
It works because strong feelings in the moment tend to crowd out the long view.
Saying no to a friend's request might feel awful in ten minutes, barely matter in ten months, and be forgotten in ten years.
Quitting a secure job might feel terrifying in ten minutes and still turn out to be the best move you ever made.
The test doesn't give you the answer.
It just puts all three time frames on the table at once.
The second is the premortem, another idea from Gary Klein.
You've probably heard of a post-mortem, where you look back on what went wrong.
A premortem does it in advance.
Imagine it's a year from now and your decision has turned out badly.
Then ask yourself, what went wrong?
Give yourself a moment to come up with the story.
This works better than asking, what could go wrong?
Klein pointed to earlier research by Deborah Mitchell, Jay Russo and Nancy Pennington, published in 1989.
They found that imagining an event has already happened increased people's ability to come up with reasons for it by about thirty per cent.
Imagining failure as a fact frees your mind to see risks you'd been quietly ignoring.
If you're planning a renovation, a premortem might surface the dodgy quote, the council approval you forgot, or the budget with no room for surprises.
Let's try a quick one together.
If you're driving, just listen along and think it over later.
Think of a decision you're weighing up at the moment.
First, is it a one-way or a two-way door?
If it's two-way, what's good enough, and could you simply try it?
If it's one-way, what would you tell a friend in your shoes?
How will it look in ten minutes, ten months and ten years?
And if it all goes wrong a year from now, what's the most likely reason?
Let's recap.
Sort decisions into two-way doors, which you can make quickly and adjust, and one-way doors, which deserve slow and careful thought.
Under pressure, check whether the deadline is real, and ask what you'd tell a friend.
For the big ones, run the ten-ten-ten test and a quick premortem before you commit.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is a two-way door decision?
Answer. One you can reverse, so you can decide quickly and adjust.
Question two. What are the three time frames in the ten-ten-ten test?
Answer. Ten minutes, ten months and ten years.
Question three. In a premortem, what do you imagine?
Answer. That your decision has already failed, and then you explain why.
That's the end of Deciding Well Under Pressure. Good call finishing that one.
